explanations.answer: It's when the LORD brought them out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Moses, Israel's leader, gives in his own words: “…because in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night.” (Deuteronomy 16:1) So the month is a reminder of the day they walked out. You don't forget an anniversary like that, baker. Miss one and you'll hear about it for years.

explanations.answer: It's when the whole harvest is gathered in
explanations.explanation: Harvest does show up in this passage, friend, but later. Gathering from the threshing floor and the winepress goes with the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:13). Moses ties the month of Abib to something else: the LORD bringing Israel out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:1). Right passage, wrong feast.

explanations.answer: It's when Moses first received the law
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, never says that in this verse. The reason he gives is that in the month of Abib the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt by night (Deuteronomy 16:1). That's the whole link he draws. When the text gives one reason, I'm not going to go shopping for a second one.

Not quite, friend. Moses says the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt “by night.” (Deuteronomy 16:1) Daylight isn't in the verse at all. Honestly, a whole nation leaving in broad daylight would have been a parade, and this was no parade.
That's right, baker. Moses says the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt “by night.” (Deuteronomy 16:1) The Passover is tied to that night. Nothing in the verse says daylight.

explanations.answer: In the place the LORD will choose
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Moses says to offer the Passover sacrifice “in the place the LORD will choose as a dwelling for His Name.” (Deuteronomy 16:2) Israel doesn't pick the spot. The LORD does. Moses says it again in verse 6, so he clearly wants it to stick.

Moses actually says the opposite, friend. He says, “You are not to sacrifice the Passover animal in any of the towns that the LORD your God is giving you.” (Deuteronomy 16:5) So the hometown is out. The sacrifice goes at the place the LORD will choose.

explanations.answer: At the foot of Mount Sinai
explanations.explanation: Mount Sinai isn't mentioned in these verses, baker. Moses says the place is “the place the LORD will choose as a dwelling for His Name.” (Deuteronomy 16:2) He doesn't name the spot yet. It's the LORD's choice.

That's the word, friend. Moses says Israel left the land of Egypt “in haste.” (Deuteronomy 16:3) And he calls the unleavened bread “the bread of affliction.” Haste is when you leave the house with one shoe on and figure out the rest later.

Moses doesn't say silence, baker. He says Israel left the land of Egypt “in haste.” (Deuteronomy 16:3) That's the reason the unleavened bread comes in. Nothing in the verse says anything about how quiet they were.

Shame isn't in that verse, friend. Moses says they left Egypt “in haste.” (Deuteronomy 16:3) The bread is called “the bread of affliction,” but he never says it's about shame. Stick with what the verse says, and the verse says haste.

You got it, baker. Moses says it's so “that you may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt.” (Deuteronomy 16:3) The bread is there to help them remember. And he says for the rest of your life, so this isn't a one-year thing.

Regret isn't in the verse, friend. Moses says the bread is so they “may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt.” (Deuteronomy 16:3) The day is something to remember. He never says anything about regret.

Dread doesn't show up here, baker. Moses says it's so they “may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt.” (Deuteronomy 16:3) The word is remember. Nobody's being told to tremble over the bread.

explanations.answer: As much as the LORD has blessed them
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The freewill offering is “in proportion to how the LORD your God has blessed you.” (Deuteronomy 16:10) So the amount follows the blessing. It's not a fixed price tag.

explanations.answer: The same amount for every family
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't set one flat amount, baker. The offering is “in proportion to how the LORD your God has blessed you.” (Deuteronomy 16:10) That means it can look different from one family to the next. It's called a freewill offering for a reason.

explanations.answer: A tenth of the very first grain
explanations.explanation: No tenth is mentioned in these verses, friend. The grain only comes in as the starting point for the count: seven weeks from when the sickle first touches the standing grain (Deuteronomy 16:9). The offering itself is given “in proportion to how the LORD your God has blessed you.” (Deuteronomy 16:10)

Yes, baker! Moses says, “you shall rejoice before the LORD your God in the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name.” (Deuteronomy 16:11) This feast is a joyful one. Moses is telling the whole guest list to celebrate.

No fasting here, friend. Moses tells them, “you shall rejoice before the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 16:11) The Feast of Weeks is a celebration with a freewill offering. Nothing in the verse says to skip a meal.
Mourning isn't on the invitation, baker. Moses says, “you shall rejoice before the LORD your God.” (Deuteronomy 16:11) Nobody brings tissues to this one. The word is rejoice.

It's the other way around, friend. Moses names them right on the list: “as well as the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you.” (Deuteronomy 16:11) They're invited to rejoice before the LORD with everybody else. Nobody's left standing outside.

That's right, baker. Moses includes “the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you” in the list of people who rejoice before the LORD (Deuteronomy 16:11). He says it again for the Feast of Tabernacles (Deuteronomy 16:14). They're all invited.

Yes, friend. Moses says, “Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and carefully follow these statutes.” (Deuteronomy 16:12) That's the memory he hands them. And right with it comes the call to follow the statutes carefully.

This one is true, baker. Moses says, “Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and carefully follow these statutes.” (Deuteronomy 16:12) It's a short verse, so it's easy to blink and miss it. That's the memory he wants them holding onto.

explanations.answer: After gathering from the threshing floor and winepress
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Moses says to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days “after you have gathered the produce of your threshing floor and your winepress.” (Deuteronomy 16:13) The gathering comes first and the feast follows. Hard work first, then the party.

explanations.answer: Before the first seed goes into the ground
explanations.explanation: The order is reversed, friend. Moses says to celebrate “after you have gathered the produce of your threshing floor and your winepress.” (Deuteronomy 16:13) Planting isn't mentioned at all. This feast comes after the gathering.

explanations.answer: Right at the start of the month of Abib
explanations.explanation: Abib is where Moses started the whole speech, baker. It's the month tied to the Passover and the LORD bringing Israel out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 16:1). The Feast of Tabernacles belongs to a different moment: after they've gathered from the threshing floor and the winepress (Deuteronomy 16:13).

explanations.answer: The LORD will bless their produce and work
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, friend. Moses says, “…because the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that your joy will be complete.” (Deuteronomy 16:15) The blessing is what he points to. He never lists a second reason.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will leave the land alone
explanations.explanation: Enemies don't come up in these verses, baker. The reason Moses gives is that “the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that your joy will be complete.” (Deuteronomy 16:15) That's about the blessing on their produce and work. Nothing about their neighbors.

explanations.answer: Their debts will all be forgiven that week
explanations.explanation: Nothing about debts in this verse, friend. Moses says their joy will be complete because “the LORD your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands.” (Deuteronomy 16:15) That blessing is the reason he gives. Keep your eye on the verse and not on your bills.

That's it, baker. Moses says, “all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose.” (Deuteronomy 16:16) It's not a select few. He says all your men, so the whole group goes.

That's not how Moses puts it, friend. He says, “all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose.” (Deuteronomy 16:16) The word is all, not only. The priests aren't even named in this verse.

explanations.answer: Only the elders of each tribe
explanations.explanation: Elders aren't mentioned in this verse, baker. Moses says, “all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose.” (Deuteronomy 16:16) He says all, and he doesn't narrow it down. No leaders-only list here.

Moses says the opposite, friend. He says, “No one should appear before the LORD empty-handed.” (Deuteronomy 16:16) Each one comes with a gift. And verse 17 says it's “as he is able,” so no one has to bring more than they have.

That's right, baker. Moses says, “No one should appear before the LORD empty-handed.” (Deuteronomy 16:16) Everybody brings a gift, and Moses says it's “as he is able, according to the blessing the LORD your God has given you.” (Deuteronomy 16:17) The gift fits what each one has.
